items.prose: A market maker does 900 trades a day. Each trade's P&L has mean £0.40 and sd £6, independently of every other trade. A year has 250 trading days, and days are independent.

parts.question: What is the sd of the day's P&L, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Variances add: $900 \times 6^2 = 32{,}400$, so the sd is $\sqrt{32{,}400} = 180$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the variances of the 900 trades, then take the square root.

byKey.add-sds: You added the 900 sds. Independent trades add their variances, so the sd grows like $\sqrt{900}$.
byKey.one-trade: That is the sd of one trade. The day adds 900 of them.
byKey.variance: That is the variance of the day's P&L. Take its square root.

explain.text: Independent trades let the variances add, so the day's variance is $900 \times 36 = 32{,}400$. The sd is $\sqrt{32{,}400} = 180$, or $6 \times \sqrt{900}$. The sds themselves do not add: that would give £5,400.

parts.question: The day's mean is $900 \times 0.40 = \text{£}360$. Using the sd of £180 from part 1 and $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$, what is the approximate chance of a losing day? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Standardise a P&L of 0 with the day's mean and sd.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(2)$, the chance the day is above $-2$ sds in the mirror. A loss is the lower tail: $1 - 0.9772$.
byKey.two-tailed: You counted both tails. A losing day is only the lower one.
byKey.from-add-sds: You used an sd of £5,400, from adding the sds. With the sd of £180 a loss is 2 sds down.

explain.text: By the central limit theorem the sum of 900 trades is close to $N(360, 180^2)$. A loss means falling 2 sds below the mean, so the chance is $\Phi(-2) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228$. One trade alone loses often; the day almost never does.

parts.question: Using 0.0228 from part 2, let $X$ be the number of losing days in the year, so $X \sim \text{Bin}(250, 0.0228)$. With the continuity correction and $\Phi(1.61) = 0.9463$, what is the normal estimate of $P(X \ge 10)$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Mean $250 \times 0.0228 = 5.7$ and sd $\sqrt{5.7 \times 0.9772} \approx 2.360$, so $z = \tfrac{9.5 - 5.7}{2.360} \approx 1.61$ and the estimate is $1 - 0.9463 = 0.0537$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start the area at 9.5, then standardise with $np$ and $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(1.61)$, the area below the cut. The question asks for 10 or more: $1 - 0.9463$.
byKey.no-correction: You started the area at 10. Bar 10 stands on 9.5 to 10.5, so start at 9.5.
byKey.wrong-side: You started the area at 10.5, which leaves out bar 10. Start at 9.5.
byKey.poisson-sd: You used $\sqrt{np} = \sqrt{5.7}$ for the sd. The binomial sd is $\sqrt{np(1 - p)} \approx 2.360$.

explain.text: $X \ge 10$ starts at bar 10, which stands on 9.5 to 10.5, so the area starts at 9.5. With mean 5.7 and sd 2.360 that is $z \approx 1.61$, and $1 - \Phi(1.61) = 0.0537$. Ten losing days would be rare, if the model holds.

parts.question: Part 3's normal estimate was 0.0537, with $np(1 - p) \approx 5.57$. The exact binomial gives 0.0626 and $\text{Pois}(5.7)$ gives 0.0648. Which approximation should the desk use, and why?

options.text: The Poisson: $p$ is small and $np(1 - p)$ is well under 10, so the count leans right like a Poisson
The normal: 0.0537 is within 0.01 of the exact answer, which is close enough for any tail
options.why: It is 14% too low, and the error grows further into the tail. With $np(1 - p) \approx 5.6$ the bell is the wrong shape.

options.text: The normal: the central limit theorem makes any count over 250 days close to normal
options.why: The theorem needs enough spread. With $p = 0.0228$ the bars lean against 0, and $np(1 - p)$ is below the usual 10.

options.text: Neither: a count of losing days over a year can only be found by simulation
options.why: The exact binomial is a sum of terms you can compute. The Poisson matches it to about 0.002 here.

feedback.correct: With $p$ near 0 the count is lopsided like a Poisson: 0.0648 misses the exact 0.0626 by 0.0022, the normal by 0.0089.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the rule of thumb $np(1 - p) \ge 10$ and compare each estimate with the exact 0.0626.

explain.text: The rule of thumb asks for $np(1 - p) \ge 10$ before using the bell, and here it is about 5.6. A rare event counted over many days is the Poisson's home ground. The Poisson errs by 0.0022 and the normal by 0.0089, on the low side.

items.prose: A vendor's signal calls the direction of a share each day. Over 400 independent days it was right 216 times. With no skill each call is right with chance 0.5, so the count of right calls would be $X \sim \text{Bin}(400, 0.5)$.

parts.question: Under no skill, what is the sd of $X$? Give the exact value.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A binomial has variance $np(1 - p)$.

byKey.variance: That is the variance $np(1 - p)$. Take its square root.
byKey.share: That is the sd of the share of right calls, $\tfrac{10}{400}$. The question asks about the count.
byKey.no-q: That is $\sqrt{np} = \sqrt{200}$. The variance has the factor $1 - p = 0.5$ as well.

explain.text: A binomial has variance $np(1 - p) = 400 \times 0.25 = 100$. So the sd of the count is 10 right calls, around a mean of 200. The signal's 216 is 1.6 sds above that mean.

parts.question: Use the mean 200 and sd 10 from part 1, the continuity correction and $\Phi(1.55) = 0.9394$. What is the chance a no-skill signal makes 216 or more right calls? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Start the area at 215.5, then standardise.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(1.55)$, the area below the cut. Take it from 1.
byKey.no-correction: You started the area at 216, so $z = 1.6$. Bar 216 stands on 215.5 to 216.5.
byKey.wrong-side: You started the area at 216.5, which leaves out bar 216. Start at 215.5.
byKey.two-tailed: You counted both tails. Only a high count looks like skill here.

explain.text: 216 or more covers bars 216 upward, so the area starts at 215.5. That is $z = 1.55$ and a chance of $1 - 0.9394 = 0.0606$, about one in 16. The exact binomial tail is 0.0605.

parts.question: The vendor tested 12 independent signals and is showing you the best. Using 0.0606 from part 2, what is the chance at least one of 12 no-skill signals reaches 216? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance all 12 fall short, then take it from 1.

byKey.added: You added 12 chances of 0.0606. Chances of events that can happen together do not add.
byKey.one: That is the chance for one signal. The vendor kept the best of 12.
byKey.no-correction: That starts from 0.0548, part 2 without the continuity correction. Use 0.0606.

explain.text: Each no-skill signal falls short with chance 0.9394, independently. All 12 fall short with chance $0.9394^{12} \approx 0.4723$, so at least one reaches 216 with chance about 0.5277. The best of 12 looks skilled more often than not.

parts.question: The vendor wants a cut-off $k$ for the 12 signals. With no skill anywhere, the chance that any signal reaches $k$ right calls should be at most 0.05. That needs each signal's tail at most $1 - 0.95^{1/12} \approx 0.0043$, so $z \ge 2.63$, since $\Phi(2.63) = 0.9957$. With the continuity correction, what is the smallest $k$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $\tfrac{k - 0.5 - 200}{10} \ge 2.63$ and solve for a whole $k$.

byKey.one-signal: That gives one signal a tail of 0.05, with $z = 1.645$. Twelve signals need each tail near 0.0043.
byKey.rounded-down: At $k = 226$ the area starts at 225.5, only $z = 2.55$. Round $226.8$ up.

explain.text: With the correction, $P(X \ge k) \approx 1 - \Phi\left(\tfrac{k - 0.5 - 200}{10}\right)$, so we need $k - 0.5 \ge 226.3$. The smallest whole $k$ is 227, about 57% right. The exact binomial agrees: 227 is the first cut-off with a tail under 0.0043.

parts.question: Suppose instead a signal is truly right 54% of the time. After $n$ calls its expected $t$-ratio is about $\tfrac{(0.54 - 0.5)\sqrt n}{0.5}$, using the no-skill sd of 0.5 a call. How many calls until it reaches 2? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $\tfrac{0.04\sqrt n}{0.5} = 2$ and solve for $n$.

byKey.one-se: That makes $t$ reach 1, about 157 calls. Two standard errors need four times as many.
byKey.root: That is $\sqrt n$. Square it to get the number of calls.
byKey.one-point-96: You used 1.96 in place of 2. The question asks for $t = 2$.

explain.text: Setting $\tfrac{0.04\sqrt n}{0.5} = 2$ gives $\sqrt n = 25$, so $n = 625$ calls. The vendor's 400 calls fall short, which fits part 2's ordinary 0.0606. A 4-point edge takes more than two years of daily calls to show.

items.prose: A broker's count $X$ of rejected orders on a day is never negative. On its main venue $X$ has mean 12 and sd 4, and days are independent.

parts.question: Using only the mean, what is Markov's bound on $P(X \ge 36)$? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Markov divides the mean by the threshold.

byKey.reversed: You divided the threshold by the mean. A chance cannot exceed 1: use $\tfrac{12}{36}$.
byKey.sd: You divided the sd by the threshold. Markov uses the mean.

explain.text: Markov needs only $X \ge 0$ and its mean: $P(X \ge a) \le E[X]/a$. Here that is $\tfrac{12}{36} = \tfrac13 \approx 0.3333$. It holds for any count with mean 12, however its days are spread.

parts.question: Part 1's bound used only the mean. Now use the sd as well: what is Chebyshev's bound on $P(X \ge 36)$? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $36$ is $24 = 6\sigma$ above the mean, so the bound is $\tfrac{1}{6^2} = \tfrac{1}{36} \approx 0.0278$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count how many sds 36 lies above the mean, then use $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$.

byKey.from-zero: You measured 36 from 0, as $k = 9$ sds. Chebyshev measures from the mean 12, so $k = 6$.
byKey.markov: That is Markov's bound from part 1. Chebyshev also uses the sd.

explain.text: A count of 36 or more is at least 24 above the mean, which is $k = 6$ sds. Chebyshev gives $P(|X - 12| \ge 6\sigma) \le \tfrac{1}{36} \approx 0.0278$, and the one-sided event sits inside it. Knowing the spread cut the bound twelvefold.

parts.question: The broker opens on a new venue where the sd is still 4 but the mean $\mu$ is unknown. It will estimate $\mu$ by $\bar X_n$, the average over $n$ days. Using Chebyshev, what is the smallest $n$ with $P(|\bar X_n - \mu| \ge 1) \le 0.05$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. $\bar X_n$ has variance $\tfrac{16}{n}$; bound the miss chance by it over $1^2$.

byKey.ninety-five: You set the bound $\tfrac{16}{n}$ at most 0.95. The miss chance must be at most 0.05.
byKey.sd: You used the sd 4 in place of the variance 16. Chebyshev's bound is $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}$.
byKey.clt: That is the normal answer of the next step. Chebyshev, which assumes no shape, needs more days.

explain.text: The average has variance $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \tfrac{16}{n}$. Chebyshev with a margin of 1 bounds the miss chance by $\tfrac{16}{n}$, which is at most 0.05 once $n \ge 320$ days. The law of large numbers says the average settles; Chebyshev says how soon, for any shape.

parts.question: If the daily counts are not too lopsided, the central limit theorem makes $\bar X_n$ close to $N(\mu, \tfrac{16}{n})$. Using $P(|Z| > 1.96) = 0.05$, what is the smallest $n$ that keeps $|\bar X_n - \mu| < 1$ with chance 0.95? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Fit 1.96 standard errors, $\tfrac{4}{\sqrt n}$ each, inside the margin of 1.

byKey.rounded-down: At $n = 61$ the margin is $1.96 \times \tfrac{4}{\sqrt{61}} \approx 1.004$, just over 1. Round $61.5$ up.
byKey.one-tail: You used 1.645, which leaves 5% in one tail. A miss either way counts, so use 1.96.
byKey.no-square: That is $\sqrt n = 7.84$, rounded up. Square it to get the number of days.
byKey.chebyshev: That is Chebyshev's 320 from part 3. The normal approximation needs far fewer days.

explain.text: We need 1.96 standard errors to fit inside the margin: $\tfrac{1.96 \times 4}{\sqrt n} \le 1$, so $\sqrt n \ge 7.84$. That gives $n \ge 61.5$, so 62 days, about a fifth of Chebyshev's 320. The bell's thin tails buy the saving; Chebyshev must cover every shape.

items.prose: A fund's monthly returns have sd 4%, independently from month to month. Over 36 months its average monthly return was 1.2%.

parts.question: What is the standard error of the 36-month average, in percentage points? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The standard error is the sd over $\sqrt n$.

byKey.over-n: You divided the sd by $n = 36$. The sd of an average falls like $\sqrt n$.
byKey.sd: That is the sd of one month. An average of 36 months is much less noisy.
byKey.variance: That is the variance of the average, $\tfrac{16}{36}$. Take its square root.

explain.text: The standard error is $\sigma / \sqrt n$, the sd of an average of $n$ independent months. Here that is $\tfrac{4}{6} \approx 0.6667$ percentage points. The average of 1.2% is pinned down only to within about two-thirds of a point.

parts.question: Using 0.6667 from part 1, what is the fund's $t$-ratio against a true mean of 0? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the average by its standard error.

byKey.raw-sd: You divided by the monthly sd of 4. Divide by the standard error, 0.6667.
byKey.over-n: That divides by $\tfrac{4}{36}$, part 1's commonest slip. Use the standard error 0.6667.
byKey.inverted: You divided the standard error by the average. The $t$-ratio is the average over its standard error.

explain.text: The $t$-ratio counts standard errors: $t = \tfrac{1.2}{0.6667} \approx 1.80$. It is the same as $\tfrac{1.2\sqrt{36}}{4} = 1.8$. On its own that is short of the usual 2.

parts.question: Suppose you know nothing about the shape of the returns. With no skill, $t$ has mean 0 and sd 1. Using $t = 1.8$ from part 2, what bound does Chebyshev put on the chance a no-skill fund shows $|t| \ge 1.8$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Chebyshev with $k$ sds gives $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$.

byKey.normal: That is the normal answer, which assumes a shape. Chebyshev assumes none.

explain.text: Chebyshev with $k = 1.8$ gives $P(|t| \ge 1.8) \le \tfrac{1}{3.24} \approx 0.3086$. Luck could then produce this record up to three times in ten. The bound holds for any shape, so it cannot rule luck out.

parts.question: Now use the central limit theorem: over 36 months, $t$ is close to $N(0, 1)$ under no skill. With $\Phi(1.8) = 0.9641$, what is the chance a no-skill fund shows $|t| \ge 1.8$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find one tail, $1 - \Phi(1.8)$, then count both tails.

byKey.one-tail: That is one tail. $|t| \ge 1.8$ allows either sign, so double it.
byKey.chebyshev: That is Chebyshev's bound from part 3. The normal gives the chance itself.
byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(1.8)$, the area below 1.8. Take the two tails outside $\pm 1.8$.

explain.text: Both tails count, since $|t| \ge 1.8$ allows either sign: $2 \times 0.0359 = 0.0718$. That is about a quarter of Chebyshev's 0.3086. The bell's thin tails make luck less likely, but one record in 14 is still common.

parts.question: Suppose the fund's true edge is 1.2% a month with sd 4%. How many months until its expected $t$-ratio, $\tfrac{1.2\sqrt n}{4}$, reaches 2? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $\tfrac{1.2\sqrt n}{4} = 2$, solve, and round up.

byKey.one-se: That makes $t$ reach 1. Two standard errors need four times as many months.
byKey.rounded-down: At 44 months $t = \tfrac{1.2\sqrt{44}}{4} \approx 1.99$, just short. Round $44.4$ up.
byKey.one-point-96: You used 1.96 in place of 2. The question asks for $t = 2$.

explain.text: Setting $\tfrac{1.2\sqrt n}{4} = 2$ gives $\sqrt n \approx 6.67$ and $n \approx 44.4$. So 45 months, nearly four years, before a real edge clears 2 standard errors on average. The 36-month record of part 2 falls short of that.
